findings.claim: The guard only looks at a text's first character. So a text that contains the other layout's separator before = + - @ is never neutralised, which bypasses the D8 guard in the app's main locales. Excel opens a .csv by splitting on the Windows list separator, which is ';' in Latvian and Russian settings, as the app's own semicolon-layout label says. They are still exposed when a reader treats a quote that does not open a field as literal: Python's csv module does, and Excel's well-known 'space before the quote' behaviour suggests Excel does too. findings.area: .sav export: 8-byte short names in type-2 records
findings.claim: spss_names makes long names unique ignoring case. ReadStat, however, derives each short name from the first 8 bytes or fewer and uppercases only ASCII letters. For Latvian or Russian names that differ only in the case of a non-ASCII letter within those bytes, the file therefore holds case-insensitively duplicate variable names. SPSS and PSPP names are case-insensitive. PSPP gives the second variable a generated name (with a warning), and its long-name entry then refers to an unknown variable, so the exported variable loses its name.
